Voice Type. The categorization of singing voices by range, timbre, and tessitura, the comfortable pitch zone where a vocalist naturally sits. The six principal voice types—soprano, mezzo-soprano, alto, tenor, baritone, and bass—arise from physiological differences in vocal cord size and resonance. Voice typing is essential in opera and choral music, where roles are written for specific voice types to maximize both dramatic effect and vocal comfort.

Soprano, the highest women's voice, is split into coloratura, characterized by quick, high passages; lyric, light and expressive; and dramatic, powerful variants. Mezzo-soprano sits between soprano and alto; famous roles include Carmen and Rosina from The Barber of Seville, often roles with theatrical sass or dramatic depth. Alto, the lowest women's voice, is rarest in opera but prominent in choral and early music; technically it includes countertenor, men singing in the alto range.

Tenor, the highest men's voice, is the romantic lead in opera; famous roles include Rodolfo in La Bohème and Calaf in Turandot. It is further divided into lyric, dramatic, and heldentenor, Wagnerian and heavily orchestrated variants. Baritone sits between tenor and bass and provides character roles and sometimes leading man parts with darker emotional weight, like Rigoletto. Bass, the lowest voice, is typically cast as grandfatherly, villainous, or divine characters; basso profundo, extremely low, is prized in Russian opera.

Voice type arises from physiological factors: vocal cord length and mass determine natural pitch range; resonance of the vocal tract determines timbre qualities. Tessitura, the range where a voice sits comfortably, differs from the full range a singer can technically produce; a good role for a voice sits high in its tessitura. Mistyping singers, assigning roles outside their natural type, can damage voices and produce poor performances; experienced singers and coaches work to match singers to appropriate repertoire. The traditional six categories don't capture all variations; soprano subdivisions have proliferated, and voice types can shift with age and training as singers develop control and flexibility.
